# The question {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · The tension]{.act}

## Economists can't run experiments on the economy

We can't randomly assign people different incomes, or give one city a tax cut and another none.

. . .

So how do we measure how one economic variable moves with another? **Regression** — the primary
tool of econometrics — turns a cloud of observed data into a line we can read.

::: {.notes}
Unlike a lab science, economics works mostly with observational data. Regression is how we quantify
relationships from data we did not get to control.
:::

## Where we're going

::: {.incremental}
- **What** regression is — and why it's econometrics' main tool
- **Load & explore** economic data with pandas
- **Visualize** the relationship with a scatter plot
- **Fit** a simple regression by OLS with pyfixest
- **Interpret** the slope, intercept, and $R^2$ — in economic terms
:::

## Six ideas anchor this chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **Regression** — a statistical line of best fit through the data
- **Y vs X** — the outcome we explain ($Y$) and the explainer ($X$)
- **Intercept $\beta_0$ · slope $\beta_1$** — where the line starts, and how steep it is
- **OLS** — picks the line that minimizes the sum of *squared* residuals
- **$R^2$** — the share of variation in $Y$ the line explains (0 to 1)
- **Association $\neq$ causation** — regression measures how $Y$ and $X$ move together, not cause
:::

[The slope is almost always the number you actually care about.]{.takeaway .fragment}

# From data to a fitted line {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Act II · The investigation]{.act}

## Our question: do bigger houses sell for more?

29 house sales in Davis, California (1999). Two columns carry the story: **price** and **size**.

$$\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{size} + \varepsilon$$

[We want $\beta_1$ — the predicted change in price per extra square foot. OLS chooses $\beta_0, \beta_1$
to make the squared gaps between the dots and the line as small as possible.]{.comment}

## Step 1 — load and explore the data with pandas

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|5|7-8"}
import pandas as pd                          # pandas → load & handle tabular data

# dataset: 29 house sales in Davis, CA, 1999 (price, size, bedrooms, …)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HOUSE.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # read the Stata .dta into a DataFrame

data.head()                                  # peek at the first few rows
data.describe().round(2)                     # summary stats: mean, std, min, max, quartiles
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Mean price ≈ $253,910, mean size ≈ 1,883 sq ft; price ranges $204k–$375k. Always describe before
you model — the scale and spread make the regression interpretable later.
:::

## Step 2 — always visualize before you model

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7|8-9"}
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt               # plotting

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HOUSE.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # load the 29 Davis, CA house sales

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))      # one figure + axes
ax.scatter(data["size"], data["price"],      # x = size, y = price
           s=80, alpha=0.7, color="#22d3ee") # marker size, transparency, colour
plt.show()                                   # render the scatter plot
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

## Price rises with size — the relationship is real but loose

![Each dot is a house. The upward drift is the relationship; the vertical scatter is everything size doesn't explain.](figures/fig_1-5_01.png)

[A scatter plot is the honest first look — it shows direction and spread before any model.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Step 3 — fit the regression by OLS with pyfixest

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-7|9|10"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                     # install pyfixest in Colab (-q = quiet; not preinstalled)

import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                         # pyfixest → OLS regression, R-style formulas

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HOUSE.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # load the 29 Davis, CA house sales

fit = pf.feols("price ~ size", data=data)    # OLS: regress price on size (intercept auto-added)
fit.summary()                                # β0, β1, SEs, t, p, R²
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
pyfixest.feols is the project's estimation tool — the same `y ~ x` formula syntax as R's fixest.
One line fits the model; summary() prints the full table.
:::

## OLS draws the line: price = 115,017 + 73.77 × size

![The fitted line through the cloud, with its equation.](figures/fig_1-8_01.png)

[Slope $\beta_1 = \$73.77$/sq ft · intercept $\beta_0 = \$115{,}017$ · $R^2 = 0.62$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Reading the three numbers

::: {.incremental}
- **Slope $\beta_1 = \$73.77$** — each extra square foot is associated with about **\$74** more in price (≈ \$7,400 per 100 sq ft).
- **Intercept $\beta_0 = \$115{,}017$** — just where the line crosses $x=0$; a 0-sq-ft house isn't meaningful, so don't over-read it.
- **$R^2 = 0.62$** — size alone explains about **62%** of the price variation; the other 38% is location, condition, age, …
:::

[Report magnitude, not just significance: \$74 per square foot is the economically meaningful finding.]{.takeaway .fragment}

# Reading it right {.divider background-color="#C21E72"}

[Act III · The resolution]{.act}

## The tempting mistake — and the correction

[Objection.]{.objection} "Each square foot *adds* \$74 — so extending my house 100 sq ft adds \$7,400."

. . .

[Response.]{.rebuttal} **Association is not causation.** Bigger houses may also be better-located and
better-renovated — the slope credits size for quality's effect too. Like ice-cream sales and drownings:
both rise in summer, but one doesn't cause the other.

[Regression shows how $Y$ and $X$ move together; a causal reading needs a design that rules out the alternatives.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## What to carry forward

::: {.incremental}
- Regression is econometrics' primary tool: it quantifies how $Y$ varies with $X$.
- The simple model is $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon$; **OLS** minimizes squared residuals.
- The **slope** measures association; **$R^2$** measures fit — neither proves causation.
- The Python workflow is **load → explore → visualize → model → interpret** (`pandas`, `matplotlib`, `pyfixest`).
- Don't extrapolate beyond the data, and don't assume the sample generalizes.
:::
